messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Tariq is a 52-year-old Lebanese-American actor, widowed, who presents with a PCL-5 score of 66 following the traumatic death of his young daughter three years ago. She was killed in a crowd crush at a public festival — a community event Tariq had encouraged the family to attend. He had been separated from her in the surge of bodies, and by the time he reached her, emergency responders were already present. He could do nothing. The sounds he heard in those final moments — screaming, the particular pitch of children crying in panic — are sounds he has never been able to leave behind.

The memories themselves do not come as a coherent narrative. Instead, Tariq experiences them as photographic fragments: a freeze-frame of her face in the crowd, the colour of her jacket, his own hand reaching. These disconnected pieces resist assembly into anything that could be processed or mourned cleanly, and when they surface — which they do without warning — they bring with them a wave of intense guilt so consuming that Tariq has described it as a physical weight pressing on his chest. The fragmented, guilt-saturated quality of these recollections has made him terrified of stillness, because stillness is when the images arrive most forcefully. That fear has quietly reorganised his life: he avoids being alone in a room or building for any length of time, filling his schedule and his space with other people not out of connection but out of a desperate need to keep the memories at a manageable distance. Yet paradoxically, the avoidance of solitude has kept him from ever sitting with the memories long enough to integrate them, so they remain raw and ungoverned, ready to flood him at the next trigger.

His work as an actor presents particular difficulty. Rehearsal rooms, green rooms, and sets are full of ambient sound — and on more than one occasion, a child's crying from somewhere in the building, or a piece of incidental music resembling sounds from that day, has stopped him mid-scene. When these auditory triggers land, the threat system activates immediately: his concentration dissolves, he is flooded with fear, horror, and shame simultaneously, and he finds it impossible to believe he is safe even when colleagues reassure him directly. He has come to believe that safety is simply not a category that applies to him anymore — that the world demonstrated its true nature that day, and no amount of reassurance can overwrite that knowledge. The triggered state of high arousal then makes him hypervigilant to further stimuli, so that ordinary sounds on set become potential threats, and his perceptual threshold lowers until the environment feels saturated with danger. In this state, related media — news coverage of crowd incidents, documentary footage, even fictional depictions — becomes unbearable, and he has learned to leave rooms where screens are on, to scroll past anything that might carry him back.

The appraisals Tariq holds about the event are among the most corrosive features of his presentation. He is certain that the festival organisers failed in their duty of care, that the systems meant to protect attendees were negligent, and that no one has been held accountable in any meaningful way. These beliefs — which are not without factual basis — feed a constant sense of threat and injustice that keeps his nervous system in a state of low-grade emergency. But the most painful appraisal is directed inward: he will never forgive himself for not doing more. This conviction of inaction guilt is reinforced every time the memories return, and the guilt itself deepens the sense that the world is dangerous and that he, specifically, cannot be trusted to protect those he loves. The people-pleasing behaviour that has developed — going along with whatever others want, never asserting a need, making himself agreeable and undemanding — feels to him like a form of penance, but it also sustains a posture of helplessness that confirms his worst beliefs about his own agency.

What finally brought Tariq to seek help was a rehearsal last month in which a child actor on set began crying during a break. He walked off the production without explanation and sat in his car for two hours, unable to move. He has not returned to that job. He comes to therapy hoping, in his words, to be able to work again — but what he is most afraid of is that the guilt will turn out to be deserved.
